item.title: 5 Self-Care Habits Every College Student Needs to Thrive
item.description:
Education

5 Self-Care Habits Every College Student Needs to Thrive

Beyond grades and internships: Why wellness, connection, and awe count.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Sleep, food, and movement are the foundation for energy, mood, and focus in school.
  • Real community in college takes courage and planning, not just luck.
  • Awe—through nature, hobbies, or faith—boosts students’ meaning and well-being.

Students and families have such high expectations for college: find a passion, learn as much as possible, make lifelong friends, have great internships that turn into great jobs, and maybe even have some fun. But too often, students put caring for themselves as a whole person—their self-care—on the back burner.

Lack of adequate self-care is one reason many students complain of being stressed out, exhausted all the time, and not as motivated as they would like to be. We aren’t born knowing how to make reasonable schedules that balance everything: study, work, play, social connection, and self-care.

Source: Mia Nosanow

Most, if not all, students struggle in some way with how to develop a balanced lifestyle that supports their mental health. My hope is that prioritizing these five wellness areas will provide habits that students can personalize in order to flourish in college.

Sleep

Our culture makes it easy to disregard the need for enough restorative sleep. While most of us need seven to nine hours each night to both feel and perform at our best, athletes and others may need as much as 10 hours per night. Even if we feel we can get by on less than what we know is ideal, research shows that we perform worse on tests and other measures with this level of sleep. Adding a nightly wind-down period and enough hours to sleep to our schedules is essential.

Food

Proper nutrition and digestion lead to more energy, which in turn leads to more effective learning and better moods, so it's vitally important to create food habits that work. Scheduling in enough time to make decent meals or get to the dining hall can be like solving a puzzle. Try to think outside the box about how and where to get food.

Movement

Like proper nutrition, exercise is a subject that generates almost as many opinions as there are writers. That said, the best exercise is the one that you will do regularly and that you enjoy—no need to go to the gym if you love biking or social dancing. The general recommendation is to move in some manner on a daily basis and include a more rigorous workout one to three times per week. Having a plan for when and how you accomplish your movement makes it much more likely that it will happen.

Community

A PhD in psychology isn’t needed to know that good relationships are indispensable to mental health and even to physical health and longevity. We are hardwired for bonding, yet it can be hard to bond in healthy ways, which is something many students struggle with in college. Gently going outside our comfort zones, patience, persistence, and planning are all key in the journey to “finding your people.”

Awe

“Awe engages five processes—shifts in neurophysiology, a diminished focus on the self, increased prosocial relationality, greater social integration, and a heightened sense of meaning—that benefit well-being,” according to recent research. We intuitively know that being outside enjoying nature—either by ourselves or with others—benefits our mood and renews our energy. Psychology researchers have found that a wide variety of hobbies provide well-being benefits, including art making, fine arts viewing, old-school crafts, and more. For those with a faith tradition, practicing it can improve mental health by building a sense of belonging, practicing gratitude, and understanding that there is something greater than ourselves. Scheduling in awe activities to our week shows wide-ranging benefits and can be tailored to each individual's preferences.

It’s no mystery why balancing all the elements of life in college is so hard. Class periods and hours needed to study genuinely take up a lot of time. When we can add the above five self-care categories to our schedules, we will have a better chance to both succeed and thrive in college.

item.title: What Happens After the Rescue?
item.description:
Trauma

What Happens After the Rescue?

New research reveals how helping can retraumatize trafficking survivors.

Posted August 4, 2026

Do you remember the feeling when you read a human trafficking sign in the airport restroom?

The sign asks questions like, “Are you being forced to work against your will?” and “Are you hurt, threatened, or being kept from leaving?” Further down, it says, “You are not alone. Help is available…Call 1-888-373-7888…Text HELP to BeFree” (Department of Homeland Security).

Perhaps you read a few of the lines but felt anxious because the door wouldn’t lock and you only had 20 minutes to get to your gate on time.

Or you were confused because you didn’t understand it and thought it had nothing to do with you.

Or you nodded, prayed, and felt a little positive because you volunteer at a faith-based organization (FBO) that helps survivors.

Or you felt an immediate wrenching pain in your body because you are a trafficking survivor.

Or maybe you are a victim and felt a mixture of numbness, fear, and distrust.

Or maybe you are the perpetrator and felt smug.

Statistics reveal there are approximately 27.6 million human trafficking victims worldwide, which is greater than the entire population of Australia (National Human Trafficking Hotline, 2025). Of these estimated totals, which may be far underestimated due to the secrecy surrounding trafficking, around 6.3 million represent sex trafficking victims.

But behind every number is a real person trying to survive unimaginable abuse.

Who Causes Harm?

It is tempting to imagine that perpetrators are always strangers or obvious criminals. Yet research reminds us that perpetrators can also be trusted adults, parents, ministers, or respected leaders (Knight et al., 2026).

While most of us will never commit such horrific acts, there is another uncomfortable question worth asking: When might our own beliefs, certainty, or even good intentions unintentionally contribute to someone else's suffering?

When Helping Hurts

In the United States, faith-based organizations (FBOs) that help fight sex trafficking with shelter and recovery make up a dominant channel of support, with 63 percent of shelters identifying as Christian-affiliated (Albert, 2025). According to Albert, survivors cite that the FBOs helped them gain a sense of belonging and spiritual community, along with self-forgiveness.

However, an extensive qualitative study by Knight et al. (2026) found that some faith-based services can hinder healing through retraumatizing judgments and condemnations, spiritual bypassing, religious trauma, discrimination, coercive practices, and approaches that diminish survivors' agency and self-forgiveness. Survivors also described harms associated with rigid religious interpretations, exclusion, and conditions placed on care or belonging.

This isn't an argument against faith or faith-based organizations. The lesson is something far more nuanced: Healing flourishes when faith is paired with humility, trauma-informed care, and respect for a survivor's agency. And that humility begins when we are willing to ask: Could my good intentions ever harm the person in front of me?

Because healing gets hindered when helping becomes:

  • Spiritual bypassing—using faith to bypass grief, anger, trauma, or difficult emotions rather than processing them.
  • Rigid judgment—assuming we know what healing "should" look like and who is worthy of compassion, belonging, or support.
  • Loss of agency—making decisions for survivors, imposing beliefs or expectations, or overlooking their autonomy in the healing process.

The Sign We Become

The next time you notice one of those airport restroom signs, pause for just a moment. You may never know who stood in front of it before you.

  • A survivor
  • A volunteer
  • A healthcare professional
  • Someone who has never considered trafficking before
  • Someone silently wondering if help is possible

Our first responsibility is to recognize suffering. Our second is to ensure that our efforts to help do not unintentionally deepen it.

Compassion isn't only about offering support. It's also about remaining curious enough to ask whether the support we offer truly helps the person standing before us.

The sign in the airport may point someone toward help. Our response may determine whether they feel safe enough to accept it.

item.title: Stop Fighting Reality at 3 A.M.
item.description:
Mindfulness

Stop Fighting Reality at 3 A.M.

Acceptance isn't surrender. It's the only ground you can push off from.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Fighting a reality you can't change often works as avoidance—it just looks like courage.
  • Acceptance and giving up are opposites: Giving up walks out of the moment, acceptance finally walks in.
  • Acceptance is for the unchangeable. If you can move the thing, seeing clearly is the floor, not the ceiling.

There's a specific kind of 3 a.m. where you're not asleep and you're not awake. You're litigating.

I've languished in mental courtrooms during the wee hours of the morning many times. I’ve built a body of emotional case law against something that had already happened, or rehearsed the argument I'd win, if only reality would show up to court (hopefully with unprepared counsel). It never does. Reality doesn't take meetings. It doesn't read your brief. And there I was anyway: a psychologist who knows the research, filing motion after motion against a verdict that was already final.

There I go with legal analogies (my semester in law school clearly needed some airtime).

We call that fighting the “good fight.” We're proud of it, even. Don't give up, we tell each other. Keep fighting. But watch what the fight is actually doing at 3 a.m. It isn't changing the outcome; it's keeping me busy enough not to feel it.

Fighting a reality you cannot change is often the most respectable way we've invented to run from it. It looks like courage, but it functions like a flinch, a sophisticated one, dressed in the language of grit. In Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), this is the engine of experiential avoidance: The harder we struggle against an inner experience or an unchangeable fact, the more it runs the show. As I heard ACT co-founder Steve Hayes say at a conference once, what we resist tends to persist, not as punishment, but as physics.

When someone says "just accept it," and everything in you recoils, I’d say that’s good. The recoil is the sane response. Because most of us hear that phrase as: give up. Go limp. Approve of the thing. Pretend it's fine. It means none of that.

Accepting a hard reality and giving up on it are not neighbors because they're opposites. Giving up abandons the moment. It walks out of the room where your life is happening. Acceptance does the harder thing: It finally walks in. It says this is what's here before deciding what to do about it. One is an exit. The other is an entrance.

Acceptance isn't the white flag. It's a compassionate yet courageous form of war paint.

But…and this is where the metaphor earns its keep, the courage isn't in the fighting. It's in stopping the fight with what already is. Psychologist and meditation teacher Tara Brach, in Radical Acceptance, calls it "the willingness to experience ourselves and our life as it is." Willingness, not approval. An active, muscular yes to reality as the ground you stand on, so you can push off from it toward something that matters. This is the opposite of good-vibes-only: You are not required to feel good about what's here. You're asked to be willing to feel it, which is a far braver thing.

A cautionary note. Acceptance is for the unchangeable. It is not an instruction to tolerate the intolerable. If the reality is a cruel job, a contemptuous relationship, an injustice you can actually move, acceptance isn't the ceiling, it's the floor. It's seeing the thing clearly enough, without the fog of the fight, to change it. You cannot make a leap if you don’t have a solid sense of footing to leap from.

Here is where the Momentology frame does its work. OWNing a moment—Only this moment, Without fixation, Noticing—begins by dropping the fixation that reality should be other than it is. Listen, Look, Leap is the sequence: Listen to what's here in all your senses, including your thoughts and emotions; Look at it without the courtroom lighting (and without fixating on blaming or shaming beliefs); and then Leap—act from what's real.

The Leap Point is that hinge exactly: the instant you stop litigating and start moving. Research has begun probing the far end of this stance: A 2025 line of work in the Journal of Positive Psychology associates amor fati, a posture of embracing one's fate, with later well-being. Worth knowing; hold it loosely. That's correlational and self-reported, a pointer, not proof of cause.

Play with this the next time you catch yourself building the case. Call it clearing the docket.

One: Name the reality in a single flat sentence, no adjectives. "The diagnosis is real." Not "the unfair, unbelievable, devastating diagnosis." Just the fact.

Two: Find where you're gripping it—jaw, fists, the held breath. Your body has been in the courtroom too.

Three: Say the willing line, and mean it as a beginning and not a defeat: "This is what's here. I'm willing to have it."

Four: Ask one question, and let it land in your chest rather than your head: Given that this is true, what is one move toward what matters—in the next hour?

Ten seconds. No props. It won't make the hard thing stop being hard, but it gets you back into the room where you can do something about it.

When is your mind? Mine is often nexting with fantasized fallouts and wicked things coming my way. The practice isn't to never litigate. It's to notice you've left the room, and walk back in, again and again, until walking back in gets faster.

Because acceptance was never a switch you flip once and leave flipped. It's a skill, trainable as any other, that you will practice badly and then less badly for the rest of your life. It is not the moment you surrender the fight for change. It's the moment change becomes possible at all.

The next time you're at the counter at 3 a.m., prepping your case, notice your hands. Are they clenched into a fist, or open enough, finally, to pick something up, to receive something you just might need?

item.title: What Therapists Miss When Clients Bring the Sacred
item.description:
Spirituality

What Therapists Miss When Clients Bring the Sacred

Psychological bypassing, and how to assess without instant pathologizing.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • When the sacred is met only clinically, people may stop disclosing rather than object.
  • Missing psychosis or delirium is the mirror error, and it carries its own serious cost.
  • Discernment, rather than immediate interpretation, is what the work asks of clinicians.

This is Part 2 of a series about spiritual and psychological bypassing. Read Part 1 here.

In a previous post, I discussed how spiritual bypassing describes the use of transcendence to avoid psychological and emotional pain. I suggested that psychological bypassing is the reverse: the use of clinical or therapeutic language to avoid the sacred and numinous.

The question I ended on was not whether to psychologically interpret this, but whether the interpretation serves the person in front of us or protects the clinician from material they were not trained to hold.

Source: Clark University, 1909 / Wikimedia Commons / Public Domain

Where the Reflex Comes From

Jung wrote about how Freud once urged him to make a dogma of his sexual theory, as an unshakeable bulwark against what Freud called the "black tide of mud of occultism." Two of the founding figures of modern psychotherapy split, in part, over exactly this issue. Jung treated the numinous as material to be acknowledged, understood, and integrated; Freud treated spiritual explanations as a threat to the scientific standing of the entire psychological enterprise and something that ought to be dismissed.

The second view eventually won the institutions, and most clinicians were trained within its assumptions without ever being told they were, in fact, assumptions. That is worth knowing, because a reflex you can trace is a reflex you can compassionately change and work with.

What It Costs When the Spiritual Is Discredited

Clients learn quickly which parts of their lives are welcome in a therapy room, and which parts produce a certain stillness in the clinician's face. Most people route around the second category, and they do it without complaint or feedback; the therapist simply never hears about that part of their life again, and usually never finds out that they lost it.

The second cost is to the psyche itself. When someone's spiritual life becomes active, it is often a signal that something is moving, even when the presentation is painful. Material of this kind tends to arrive at thresholds: a death, diagnosis, relationship ending, or vocation collapsing.

The transpersonal psychologist Dr. David Lukoff describes mystical experiences as often involving ecstatic mood, a sense of enhanced understanding or connection, heightened sensitivity, perceptual change, and visions carrying mythological themes of death, rebirth, journey, or cosmic conflict. He also distinguishes these from classical schizophrenic delusions, where a person may believe their brain has been removed or that a stranger is impersonating their spouse.

article continues after advertisement

Pinning an experience down too early is therefore risky: The psychological explanation may simply be wrong, and the person then carries that wrong formulation as though it were the only truth about themselves. Of course, mystical and psychotic features can also overlap, which is why assessing for risk and stabilization remains imperative.

The Opposite Error Is Also Real

I want to be careful here, because the mirror error can also be dangerous. Missing a first psychotic episode, an emerging mania, or a delirium with a medical cause can cost someone years of their life. A clinician who romanticizes every unusual experience is not practising depth or transpersonal psychology; they are arguably practising negligence with better vocabulary.

None of this calls for less assessment, but it does call for assessment that does not begin from the assumption that a spiritual or mystical experience is inherently pathological. Some mystical experiences, even when overlapping with psychotic features, can still offer unexpected opportunities for positive and long-lasting growth when worked with skillfully.

Source: Vitaly Gariev/Unsplash

Working With What Arrives

Discernment is the entire task. Four things I would offer to therapists and clinicians reading this:

1. Ask what it was like before asking what it means. Interpretation is not the problem; premature interpretation is. Staying with the texture of an experience for longer than feels comfortable often reveals whether it wants to be interpreted at all. It also shows you what the experience is doing in this person's life right now.

2. Notice when the psychological reduction is protecting you. There is a difference between a formulation offered because it serves the person and one reached for because the material is unfamiliar. If you find yourself interpreting quickly, that is a red flag.

3. Let the category remain open. A dream, synchronicity, or a moment of spiritual contact does not have to be pinned down as a defence, symptom, or even a revelation. Some material asks to be held rather than settled, sometimes across many sessions. Clinicians are trained toward closure, and this is one of the places where premature closure costs more than it returns.

article continues after advertisement

4. Assess context rather than leaning on reflex. Lukoff's work on distinguishing mystical experience from psychosis offers usable markers: assess functioning before the episode, whether onset was acute, and whether the person's orientation to the experience is exploratory rather than purely terrified. Alongside these, the ordinary clinical questions still apply. Is the person sleeping? Is functioning deteriorating? Is there a substance involved, a medical cause, or a risk to their safety, etc.?

None of this requires a clinician to hold any metaphysical beliefs, but it does require that we stop treating our own explanatory frame as the only floor of reality rather than one useful description of it. Curiosity, open-mindedness, and a willingness to build one's psycho-spiritual and mythopoetic literacy go a long way when working with spiritual and religious clients.

Some of what people bring us is genuinely a symptom or a survival defence, and that is exactly what makes this so hard. Some of it is also a psyche doing what psyches have done for as long as there have been people, which is to speak in symbol, image, and altered states of consciousness at the thresholds of transformation. Holding both possibilities open at once is uncomfortable, but it is the job of anyone who wishes to provide ethical and efficacious care.

For anyone who has had their own mystical experience handed back to them as a symptom: The caution you learned in that room was intelligent, and it does not have to be permanent. There really are clinicians in whose offices all of it is welcome, including a propensity for spiritual or mystical experiences.
